title: Epistemic humility plot synopsis
text:
Nari, a low-status apprentice sky-reader, witnesses a violation in the sacred count: the seventh star in the seventh cluster moves wrong. Afraid that the fault may be hers, she checks the lens, repeats the count, and preserves the result on her slate. The anomaly remains. Master Orem, whose lifetime of experience has taught him to trust the inherited order and fear departures from it, suppresses the warning rather than treat a single contradiction as reason to overturn established truth. The lens then shows a repeatable correspondence between the wrong-moving star and the forbidden lower temple beneath the God-Stone, and Nari’s curiosity outweighs her fear.

Nari descends into forbidden temple spaces and discovers that the inherited model is incomplete, but not what should replace it. Beneath the public sacred order, the underside of the God-Stone and the lower chamber exhibit precise, repeatable correspondences with the broken seven-and-seven count. Each observation rewards Nari’s curiosity while making the phenomenon more frightening: she can establish patterns and consequences, yet cannot determine what the system is, what it is for, or what kind of agency might be involved. By the time Orem calls to her from above, Nari has begun to understand why someone could learn to fear inquiry without accepting that fear as a reason to stop.

In the final confrontation, Orem’s accumulated fear and inherited warning meet Nari’s curiosity, evidence, and growing dread. He reveals enough of the experiences behind his caution to make his resistance credible, while the chamber continues the broken count in ways neither of them can explain. As the pattern continues, neither action nor restraint can be shown to be safe. Orem confronts the possibility that fear has protected him by restricting what he was willing to learn, but also cost him knowledge he might otherwise have pursued. Nari confronts the opposite danger: curiosity can reveal real things that may have been safer left unknown. She chooses to complete or permit the final observed pattern without claiming that continuing is wiser than stopping. The God-Stone, lower chamber, and wrong-moving star enter a synchronized correspondence, and the answering light comes. Neither character is vindicated, and neither reaches the balance between curiosity and fear that the encounter suggests may be necessary. Orem is left with remorse for what fear may have kept him from knowing; Nari is left with a new understanding that knowledge itself can carry consequences. Both have moved toward the missing half of the other, but neither achieves equilibrium or comprehension.
